hints.title: Maximum Project Headcount Identification
hints.text: Determine the maximum number of assigned employees across any project, then return all project identifiers achieving that count.

hints.title: Group Count with Subquery Ceiling
hints.text: Group project records by project identifier and filter the groups using a having clause equal to the global maximum count.

hints.title: Project Headcount Query Blueprint
hints.text: select project_id from Project group by project_id having count(employee_id) = (select count(employee_id) from Project group by project_id order by count(employee_id) desc limit 1).

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT project_id
FROM Project
GROUP BY project_id
HAVING COUNT(employee_id) = (
    SELECT COUNT(employee_id)
    FROM Project
    GROUP BY project_id
    ORDER BY COUNT(employee_id) DESC
    LIMIT 1
);
```

complexity.notes: Grouping assignments and finding the maximum via scalar subquery executes in linear-logarithmic time.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Hardcoding a single project identifier ignores possible ties across top projects.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Having filter against maximum subquery cleanly handles ties without row-number windowing.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Handling ties properly when multiple projects share the maximum headcount.

import pandas as pd

def project_employees_ii(project: pd.DataFrame, employee: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    counts = project.groupby('project_id')['employee_id'].count().reset_index()
    max_count = counts['employee_id'].max()
    return counts[counts['employee_id'] == max_count][['project_id']]
solutions.approach: Pandas Groupby Count and Max Filtering
